name: Nyāya

tradition.text: from the sage Gautama Akṣapāda (no fixed date in the tradition)

scholarly.text: Nyāya Sūtra redacted c. 2nd–3rd c. CE; commentarial line from the 5th c.; merged with Vaiśeṣika from c. the 10th–11th c.; continued as Navya-Nyāya from the 14th c.

transmissions_received.what: the ontology of categories (substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence), atomism, and the account of the self's qualities
transmissions_received.evidence: Vātsyāyana acknowledges the six Vaiśeṣika categories as further objects of knowledge (NBh 1.1.9) and cites the Vaiśeṣika account of the yogin's perception of the self (NBh 1.1.3, cf. VS 9.13); later manuals are explicitly 'for the doctrines of Kaṇāda and Nyāya' (Tarkasaṅgraha).

transmissions_received.what: religious affiliation of several authors (Śaiva / Pāśupata)
transmissions_received.evidence: Uddyotakara is called a Pāśupata teacher in the Nyāyavārttika colophon; Vācaspati's Tātparyaṭīkā opens by invoking Pinākin (Śiva); Bhāsarvajña's Nyāyasāra ends with a Śaiva account of the path (moderate/low confidence).

transmissions_given.what: its categories, method and problems, recast by Gaṅgeśa
the theory of debate and inference that Buddhist logicians criticized and reshaped (Dignāga against Vātsyāyana)
the vocabulary of pramāṇa and the rules of debate used by all later Vedānta schools

distinctive_positions: The highest good (niḥśreyasa) is attained from knowledge of the truth of sixteen categories (NS 1.1.1), above all of the twelve objects of knowledge beginning with the self (NS 1.1.9).
Bondage runs from false knowledge through faults, activity and birth to pain; removing false knowledge by knowledge of truth removes the rest and yields liberation (NS 1.1.2).
Four means of knowledge — perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony (NS 1.1.3); tradition, presumption, inclusion and absence are reduced to these (NS 2.2.1–2).
The self is an eternal, all-pervading substance distinct from body, senses, mind and cognition; desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain and cognition are its marks (NS 1.1.10); selves are many.
The mind (manas) is one per body and atomic, which is why cognitions do not arise simultaneously (NS 1.1.16, 3.2.56, 3.2.59).

Liberation (apavarga) is absolute release from pain (NS 1.1.22), in which — on the mainstream view — the self has neither pleasure nor cognition (NBh 1.1.22); Bhāsarvajña dissents, holding that eternal bliss is experienced.
Validity of cognition is extrinsic (parataḥ); error is misplaced apprehension (anyathākhyāti).

Īśvara is a distinct self, free of demerit, false knowledge and heedlessness, who assists human effort and makes action fruitful (NS 4.1.19–21; NBh); later he is proved by inference as maker of the world (Udayana, NK 5.1) and as author of the Veda, whose validity is like that of mantra and medicine because its speaker is reliable (NS 2.1.69).
Effects are new beginnings not pre-existing in their causes (ārambha / asatkārya); the whole is a new substance distinct from its parts (NS 2.1.31–37, 4.2.4–17).

Realism: external objects, universals, relations and enduring things are real; momentariness, idealism and the thesis that everything lacks own-nature are refuted (NS 3.2.10–17, 4.1.25–40, 4.2.26–37).

A developed theory of debate: honest discussion (vāda), wrangling (jalpa) and cavilling (vitaṇḍā), with pseudo-reasons, quibbles, futile rejoinders and points of defeat; jalpa and vitaṇḍā are permitted to protect truth like a thorn-fence around a sprout (NS 4.2.50).
Sound is a non-eternal quality of ākāśa; the relation of word and meaning is conventional (NS 2.1.56–57, 2.2.13ff.).
summary: Nyāya ('method', 'reasoning') is the Vedic darśana of the means of valid knowledge and of reasoned debate, founded on Gautama Akṣapāda's Nyāya Sūtra and developed by Vātsyāyana, Uddyotakara, Vācaspati Miśra, Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, Bhāsarvajña and Udayana. It teaches that liberation — absolute release from pain — follows from knowledge of the truth about the self and the other objects of knowledge, won by the means of knowledge, reasoning, study, discussion and yoga. From about the 10th–11th c. it merged with Vaiśeṣika into a single realist system, and from Gaṅgeśa (14th c.) continued as Navya-Nyāya.

name: Vaiśeṣika

scholarly.text: Vaiśeṣika Sūtra core perhaps c. 1st c. BCE – 1st c. CE; Praśastapāda c. 6th c. CE; merged with Nyāya from c. the 10th–11th c.

transmissions_received.what: the Nyāya analysis of the means of knowledge and debate, in the syncretic manuals (Śivāditya, Keśava Miśra, Annambhaṭṭa)
transmissions_received.evidence: Saptapadārthī; Tarkabhāṣā; Tarkasaṅgraha ('for the doctrines of Kaṇāda and Nyāya').

transmissions_given.what: the ontology of categories and atoms
a categorial ontology, extended with capacity, similarity and number
the six categories named at the opening of the Caraka Saṃhitā (direction debated)

distinctive_positions: Dharma is that from which prosperity (abhyudaya) and the highest good (niḥśreyasa) result (VS 1.1.2); the authority of the Veda rests on its being 'the statement of that' (VS 1.1.3).

Reality is analysed into categories (padārtha): substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity and inherence — six in Praśastapāda and the Upaskāra recension of the sūtras — with absence added as a seventh in later works (Udayana's Lakṣaṇāvalī, Śivāditya's Saptapadārthī).
Nine substances: earth, water, fire, air, ākāśa, time, space, self and mind (VS 1.1.4).
Twenty-four qualities (Praśastapāda), seventeen named in the sūtra (VS 1.1.5) and seven more included by its word 'ca'; five kinds of motion (VS 1.1.6).
Earth, water, fire and air consist of eternal, partless, spherical atoms (paramāṇu) that combine into dyads and larger wholes; what exists without a cause is eternal (VS 4.1.1, 7.1.26).
Ultimate particularity (viśeṣa) distinguishes each eternal substance — traditionally connected with the school's name.
Only two means of knowledge: perception and inference; verbal knowledge is explained as inference (VS 9.18–19 in Candrānanda's recension; Praśastapāda).

Motions without visible cause — the needle's approach to a magnet, the ascent of sap, fire's upward flame, the first motion of atoms and minds, and the mind's departure at death and entry at birth — are caused by the unseen (adṛṣṭa) (VS 5.1.15, 5.2.8, 5.2.14, 5.2.19).

Yoga is the state in which, the mind resting in the self, the embodied one has neither pleasure nor pain; liberation is the absence of contact with a body and the non-arising of a new one when adṛṣṭa is absent (VS 5.2.17, 5.2.20).
The world is periodically dissolved and recreated by the will of Maheśvara acting through the adṛṣṭa of selves (Praśastapāda).
Heat transforms qualities at the level of atoms (pīlupāka), against Nyāya's view that the whole is baked (piṭharapāka).
summary: Vaiśeṣika is the Vedic darśana of categorial analysis and atomism founded on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika Sūtra and systematized by Praśastapāda. It explains dharma as the source of prosperity and the highest good, and holds that knowledge of the truth of the categories — through their similarities and dissimilarities — produced by dharma leads to liberation. Its commentators (Vyomaśiva, Śrīdhara, Udayana) made it theistic and joined it to Nyāya; after the 11th c. it survives mainly within syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika.
notes: Status 'absorbed': Vaiśeṣika ontology is still studied, but within Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika manuals.

name: Navya-Nyāya

scholarly.text: from Gaṅgeśa (first half of the 14th c.) to the present

transmissions_received.evidence: Gaṅgeśa's four khaṇḍas follow the four pramāṇas of NS 1.1.3; Udayana ('the Ācārya') is its constant authority.

transmissions_given.what: technical language and method of definition and refutation (e.g. Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi)
technical language, used in the critique of Nyāya itself (Vyāsatīrtha's Tarkatāṇḍava)
the analysis of verbal cognition, debated with the grammarians

distinctive_positions: Organizes philosophy around the four means of knowledge (the four khaṇḍas of the Tattvacintāmaṇi).

Analyses every cognition into qualificand (viśeṣya), qualifier (prakāra) and relation (saṃsarga), and specifies properties by their delimitors (avacchedaka), counterpositives (pratiyogin) and relations, yielding a precise technical language.
Gives exact definitions of pervasion (vyāpti) — testing and rejecting five provisional ones before its own — and of consideration (parāmarśa), subjecthood (pakṣatā) and the adjunct (upādhi).
Recognizes extraordinary sense-contacts (via the universal, via a prior cognition, and yogic) to explain the grasp of pervasion, some errors, and yogic perception.
Validity of cognition is extrinsic (Gaṅgeśa's Prāmāṇyavāda).
Liberation is the absolute cessation of pain, defined technically as a destruction of pain not co-temporal with any prior absence of pain in the same self (Muktivāda).
The denotative power (śakti) of a word is the Lord's convention that 'this meaning is to be understood from this word'; verbal cognition requires expectancy, compatibility, proximity and intention.
Raghunātha Śiromaṇi re-examines the traditional list of categories (Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa).
summary: Navya-Nyāya ('New Nyāya') begins with Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya's Tattvacintāmaṇi in Mithilā (14th c.) and flourished there and, from Raghunātha Śiromaṇi (c. 1500), in Navadvīpa in Bengal. It restates Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika doctrine in a precise technical language for analysing cognitions and their contents; this language became the common idiom of later Sanskrit learned discourse (Vedānta, Mīmāṃsā, grammar, law and poetics).
notes: The tradition's accounts of the rivalry between Mithilā and Navadvīpa (e.g. Vāsudeva Sārvabhauma carrying the Tattvacintāmaṇi to Navadvīpa from memory; Raghunātha's debate with Pakṣadhara) are recorded in the teacher entries at low confidence.
